                    ### Question
                    A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. The exploration is normal, except for the presence of bilateral papilledema. Which of these tests do you think will allow you to fully confirm your diagnosis ?:

                    ### Options
                    opa. Ultrasound of supra-aortic trunks.
opb. Magnetic resonance of the skull.
opc. Electroencephalogram.
opd. Lumbar puncture.
ope. Visual evoked potentials.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The presence of bilateral papilledema suggests increased intracranial pressure, which can be associated with various intracranial pathologies. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis in this case is a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the skull, as it can identify structural abnormalities such as tumors, lesions, or other causes of increased intracranial pressure. While a lumbar puncture can assess cerebrospinal fluid and may indicate increased pressure, it is not the primary diagnostic tool for identifying structural causes. An electroencephalogram (EEG) is less relevant for structural diagnosis, and ultrasound of the supra-aortic trunks does not directly address intracranial issues. Visual evoked potentials assess visual pathway function but do not confirm intracranial pathology. Therefore, the MRI is the most definitive test to confirm the diagnosis.
